newsitem.title: UK: Dlr/yen takes centre stage in Europe, stg sulks.
newsitem.headline: Dlr/yen takes centre stage in Europe, stg sulks.

text.p: The yen was the latest currency to feel the heat of broad-based dollar strength in Europe on Wednesday and dollar/yen rose to its highest level since mid-May on the back of disappointing Japanese economic data.
Thin holiday-affected markets did little to dampen enthusiasm for dollars elsewhere.

The U.S. unit set its highest level against the Swiss franc in almost four years, hovered just shy of 7-1/2-year highs against the German mark and even touched its highest level in almost two months against a more subdued sterling.

Dollar/yen lead the way higher in early trade but the approach of the psychologically-important 120 level acted as a repellent, fuelling concerns about verbal protests from Japanese authorities if yen weakness accelerated much beyond there.

"The dollar/yen did get to levels where we would expect some form of Bank of Japan or Ministry of Finace commentary in support of the yen and the 120 area will act as a barrier as a result," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International.
At 1518 GMT, the dollar was trading at 118.37/42 yen compared with 117.84/89 late Tuesday but off the intraday high at 118.95 set earlier.
The trigger for yen selling was news of a bigger-than-expected 3.1 percent drop in Japanese industrial production in June and a 2.3 percent year-on-year fall in Japanese retail sales the same month.

"The sales and output data confirm that the Japanese economy remains pretty weak and will keep Bank of Japan interest rates on hold for a good bit longer than many people had been expected," said Stamenkovic.
Dollar/yen collapsed more than 10 percent in May as Japanese officials threatened action on the foreign exchanges to support an ailing yen and concerns about a Japanese rate rise grew.
Profit taking on dollar/yen was exaggerated in late trading by a spate of market rumours, a reluctance to take on 120 and technical resistance just above 119, traders said.

Talk of the imminent resignation of U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin were dismissed by traders but unconfirmed reports that U.S. car makers had called on the U.S. government to start "Super 301" trade law procedures against Japan also weighed.
Chartists, meantime, were wary of 119 yen because it is a 50 percent reversal of the May to June dollar decline.
"I would expect, if dollar/yen gets to 120, to see words from Japan," said Jane Edwards, economist at Lehman Brothers.

Dollar strength elsewhere was underpinned in part today by fresh buoyancy in U.S. stock and bond markets but analysts said the interest rate expectations that are fueling the asset market rally may be sowing the seeds of the dollar's eventual downfall.
The yield spread between 10-year U.S. and German government bonds declined to 65 basis points today, in sharp contrast to a spread in excess of 120 basis points earlier this year.

Nervousness about a potential rise in German interest rates, meantime, was stoked by Bundesbank council memeber Hans-Juergen Koebnick late Tuesday and his comments helped keep dollar/mark shy of new peaks.

Koebnick said the Bundesbank could tighten money market liquidity if recent mark weakness persisted and raised the possibility of the bank reverting to variable rate repurchase tenders as a way of allowing market rates to tick higher.
The next Bundesbank repo tender is on August 12.
Elsewhere, sterling stayed subdued below 3.00 marks amid doubts about whether next week's Bank of England meeting would sanction higher UK rates, analysts said.
Traders said sterling sales versus the dollar were key today and the technical picture there looks poor.
